results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
`QOSMaxJobsPerUser` means the job is pending because the requested QOS has reached its per-user job count limit.

Related QOS pending reasons are the same pattern: the scheduler is telling you a limit defined on the QOS is blocking start or submission.

Common ones:

- `QOSMaxJobsPerUser`
  - Your user already has the maximum allowed number of jobs for that QOS.
  - This is a per-user count limit on jobs.

- `QOSMaxSubmitJobPerUser`
  - Your user has reached the maximum number of submitted jobs allowed in that QOS.
  - This usually counts jobs in the queue, not just running ones.

- `QOSGrpJobsLimit`
  - The QOS-wide aggregate job limit has been reached.
  - This is not just your user; all jobs using that QOS count toward it.

- `QOSGrpSubmitJobsLimit`
  - The QOS-wide submitted-job limit has been reached.

- `QOSMaxWallDurationPerJobLimit`
  - The requested time limit is too large for that QOS.

- `QOSMaxCpuPerUserLimit`, `QOSMaxNodePerUserLimit`, `QOSMaxTresPerUser`
  - Your user is at the QOS limit for CPUs, nodes, or TRES resources.

- `QOSGrpCpuLimit`, `QOSGrpNodeLimit`, `QOSGrpTres`
  - The QOS aggregate limit for CPUs, nodes, or TRES has been reached across users/jobs.

How to read them:

- `Max...PerUser` = a per-user QOS ceiling.
- `Grp...` = a shared pool limit for everyone using that QOS.
- `Submit` = limit on queued/submitted jobs.
- without `Submit`, often it refers to active/schedulable job/resource limits.
- `PerJob` = this single job requests more than the QOS allows.

Important nuance from Slurm docs: a pending job shows one reason that the scheduler encountered, not necessarily every blocking reason.

Practical interpretation:

- If you see `QOSMaxJobsPerUser`, reduce the number of your active jobs in that QOS or wait for some to finish.
- If you see `QOSMaxSubmitJobPerUser`, reduce queued job count.
- If you see `QOSGrpJobsLimit`, the whole QOS is saturated even if your own usage is low.

Where these come from:

- Slurm job reason codes define the pending reason strings.
- QOS/resource limit docs describe how QOS limits are applied.
- With some configurations, limits can cause a job to pend; with `DenyOnLimit`, some requests can be rejected at submission instead of pending.

If you want, I can also give you a quick mapping table of:
`QOS...` vs `Assoc...` vs `Partition...` pending reasons.

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
`QOSMaxJobsPerUser` means the job is pending because the selected QOS has reached its per-user job-count limit.

In practice:

- the job requested a QOS, or inherited one
- that QOS defines a maximum number of jobs allowed per user
- this user already has that many jobs counted against the QOS
- so Slurm keeps the new job pending until one of those jobs leaves the counted set

Related QOS pending reasons commonly follow the same naming pattern and point to limits enforced by the QOS rather than by the user/account association alone.

Common related QOS reasons:
- `QOSMaxJobsPerUser` — too many jobs for this user in that QOS
- `QOSMaxSubmitJobPerUser` — too many submitted jobs for this user in that QOS
- `QOSMaxWallDurationPerJobLimit` — requested time limit is above the QOS max
- `QOSMaxCpuPerJobLimit` — requested CPUs exceed the QOS max per job
- `QOSMaxNodePerJobLimit` — requested node count exceeds the QOS max per job
- `QOSMaxMemoryPerJob` or similar max-memory reason — requested memory exceeds the QOS limit
- `QOSGrpJobsLimit` — the QOS-wide aggregate jobs limit has been reached
- `QOSGrpCpuLimit`, `QOSGrpNodeLimit`, `QOSGrpMemoryLimit`, `QOSGrpGRES`/TRES-style reasons — aggregate QOS resource limit reached
- `QOSMin*` reasons — the request is below a minimum required by the QOS
- `QOSUsageThreshold` — usage/fairshare threshold for that QOS is blocking dispatch

Useful distinction:
- `QOSMax...` usually means a per-job or per-user maximum tied to the QOS
- `QOSGrp...` usually means a shared aggregate cap across all jobs in that QOS
- `AssocMax...` / `AssocGrp...` are similar ideas, but enforced from the account/user association instead of the QOS

How to interpret `QOSMaxJobsPerUser` specifically:
- it is about job count, not priority
- raising priority will not bypass it
- the job will start only when the count drops, or if the job uses a different permitted QOS, or if admins change the QOS limit

Where these limits come from:
- QOS definitions are managed in Slurm accounting/QOS configuration
- QOS limits can override user/account/cluster/partition association limits
- partition-attached QOS can also impose limits, with precedence affected by QOS flags such as `OverPartQOS`

If you want, I can also explain the difference between:
- `QOSMaxJobsPerUser` vs `QOSMaxSubmitJobPerUser`
- `QOS...` vs `Assoc...`
- job-count limits vs TRES/resource limits

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
`QOSMaxJobsPerUser` means the job is pending because the requested QOS has a per-user job-count limit, and that limit has been reached for that user.

In practice:

- Slurm checks limits attached to the job’s QOS.
- `MaxJobsPerUser` on that QOS caps how many jobs one user may have under that QOS.
- If submitting or starting another job would exceed that cap, the pending reason can appear as `QOSMaxJobsPerUser`.

Related QOS pending reasons are the same pattern applied to other QOS-enforced limits. Common ones include:

- `QOSMaxJobsPerUser` — user hit the QOS job-count limit.
- `QOSMaxSubmitJobPerUser` — user hit the QOS submit-count limit.
- `QOSMaxWallDurationPerJobLimit` — requested time limit is too large for that QOS.
- `QOSMaxCpuPerJobLimit` / `QOSMaxNodePerJobLimit` / similar `QOSMax*PerJobLimit` — the job request itself exceeds a per-job QOS maximum.
- `QOSGrp*Limit` reasons — the QOS has a group/aggregate limit already consumed, such as total CPUs, nodes, jobs, or TRES for all jobs using that QOS.
- `Max*PerAccount` reasons — similar limit enforcement, but tied to the QOS limit as applied per account.

Useful distinction:

- `QOSMaxJobsPerUser` is about how many jobs a user may have with that QOS.
- `QOSMaxSubmitJobPerUser` is about how many submitted jobs a user may queue under that QOS.
- `QOSGrp*` reasons are aggregate caps shared across multiple jobs/users/accounts, depending on the configured limit.

Also important: QOS limits can override normal association limits, and partition QOS limits can also apply. So a job may be blocked by a QOS even if the user/account would otherwise be allowed.

If you want, I can also explain how `QOSMaxJobsPerUser` differs from `AssocMax*` and `Partition*` pending reasons.

results.prompt: Explain AssocGrpGRES and association group resource limits
results.agent_response:
`AssocGrpGRES` is a Slurm pending reason/code meaning:

- the job’s association has hit an aggregate GRES limit
- so the job cannot start until enough of that grouped GRES usage becomes available under that association limit

In Slurm, an association is typically the user/account/cluster association used for accounting and limits. Per the docs, association limits are checked in this order:

1. user association
2. account
3. cluster
4. otherwise no limit

What “group resource limits” means here:

- `Grp*` limits are aggregate caps across multiple jobs in the same association
- `GRES` means generic resources, commonly things like GPUs
- so `AssocGrpGRES` usually means the total requested or in-use GRES across all jobs for that association has reached the configured ceiling

How it differs from similar reasons:

- `AssocGrp*` = aggregate limit across the association
- `AssocMax*` = a single job request exceeds a per-job or per-node style maximum for the association

Examples:

- If an account has a group limit of 8 GPUs total, and its running jobs are already using 8 GPUs, another 1-GPU job may pend with `AssocGrpGRES`
- If a single job requests more GPUs than the association allows any one job to request, that is more in the `AssocMax*` family

Related association group limit reasons you may also see:

- `AssocGrpCPUs`
- `AssocGrpMem`
- `AssocGrpJobs`
- `AssocGrpWall`
- `AssocGrpBilling`
- `AssocGrpGRESMinutes`
- `AssocGrpGRESRunMinutes`

Those mean the same general thing, but for different aggregate resources or time-weighted usage limits.

Operationally, to resolve `AssocGrpGRES`, one of these must happen:

- some running jobs in that association finish
- the pending job requests fewer GRES
- the association/account limit is raised by an administrator
- the job is submitted under a different valid association with available quota

If you want, I can also explain how to inspect which association limit is set using `sacctmgr` and how `GrpTRES` relates to `AssocGrpGRES`.

results.prompt: Explain AssocGrpGRES and association group resource limits
results.agent_response:
`AssocGrpGRES` is a Slurm pending/denial reason that means a job is blocked by an association-level group GRES limit.

What it means:
- `Assoc` = the limit comes from the accounting association hierarchy.
- `GrpGRES` = a group limit on generic resources, such as GPUs or other configured GRES.
- In practice, the job would cause the total GRES usage for that association scope to exceed its configured cap.

Association group resource limits:
- These are limits attached to associations managed through accounting.
- Associations can exist at multiple levels:
  - user association
  - account association
  - cluster/root association
- Slurm applies association limits hierarchically. A defined limit at the first applicable level in the hierarchy is what gets enforced.

How `GrpGRES` behaves:
- It is a shared cap across the association, not just a per-job cap.
- The scheduler sums current usage in that association scope and checks whether starting the job would exceed the configured GRES limit.
- If yes, the job stays pending with a reason like `AssocGrpGRES`.

Example:
- Suppose an account has a group GPU limit of 8.
- Jobs already running under that account are using 7 GPUs total.
- A new job requests 2 GPUs.
- Starting it would raise usage to 9, so the job pends with `AssocGrpGRES`.

Common related distinctions:
- `AssocMaxGRESPerJob`: this single job asks for more GRES than allowed per job.
- `AssocMaxGRESPerUser`: the submitting user exceeds a per-user GRES cap.
- `AssocGrpGRES`: the shared association total is the issue.

Where these limits are configured:
- Via `sacctmgr` association/resource limit settings.
- Enforcement requires accounting limit enforcement to be enabled; Slurm docs note `AccountingStorageEnforce=limits` is the minimum needed for limits to be enforced.

Important GRES type nuance from Slurm docs:
- If limits are set on a specific typed GRES, like `gres/gpu:tesla=1`, and a user requests a generic GRES like `--gres=gpu:2`, that typed limit may not be enforced as expected.
- Slurm documents this as a design limitation for typed GRES enforcement.

So the short version:
- `AssocGrpGRES` = “your job cannot start because your association’s shared GRES quota is currently full or would be exceeded by this job.”

How `AssocGrpGRES` differs from related reasons
- `AssocGrp*` = aggregate/group limit has been reached
- `AssocMax*` = a single job request exceeds a configured maximum
- So:
  - `AssocGrpGRES` means “too much total GRES already in use by the association”
  - `AssocMaxGRES*` would mean “this job itself asks for more than allowed”

Examples
- If an account has a group GPU limit of 8, and running jobs already use 8 GPUs total, another GPU job can pend with `AssocGrpGRES`.
- If a user/account has a limit on another GRES type, the same logic applies.

What Slurm is checking
Slurm compares the association’s current aggregate GRES usage against configured association limits managed through accounting policies. These limits are typically managed with `sacctmgr`, and enforcement requires accounting limit enforcement to be enabled.

Useful mental model
- `Grp*` = shared pool cap for the association
- `Max*` = cap on one job / node / submission shape
- `GRES` = tracked generic resources such as GPUs

If you want, I can also explain the common related variants like:
- `AssocGrpGRESMinutes`
- `AssocGrpGRESRunMinutes`
- `AssocMaxGRESPerJob`
- QOS vs association limit differences

results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
`ReqNodeNotAvail` is a Slurm pending reason meaning the job is waiting because the nodes it needs are currently unavailable.

Common cases behind it:

- The job explicitly requested specific nodes with `--nodelist`, `--exclude`, features, constraints, or a topology/layout requirement, and the matching nodes are not usable now.
- Matching nodes are in unavailable states such as:
  - `DOWN`
  - `DRAIN`
  - `FAIL`
  - `FAILING`
  - `FUTURE`
- Matching nodes are in or affected by maintenance or reservation conditions.
- Matching nodes are being rebooted, powered up/down, or otherwise not ready for scheduling.
- The scheduler sees the nodes as unavailable because they are reserved for a higher-priority purpose or planned by backfill.

Common node-availability indicators you may see in Slurm outputs include:

- `down` / `drain` / `fail` style states
- maintenance reservation markers
- reboot / power transition markers
- planned-for-higher-priority-job markers

A practical interpretation:

- If your job is flexible, `ReqNodeNotAvail` often means the request is too restrictive.
- If your job must use certain nodes, it usually means those nodes need admin intervention or must return to service.

Typical things to check:

- `squeue -j <jobid>` for the pending reason
- `scontrol show job <jobid>` for detailed constraints and requested nodes
- `sinfo -R` to see down/drained nodes and reasons
- `sinfo` to see node states and partition availability

Common human-readable node reasons behind the unavailable state:

- hardware issue
- filesystem or network problem
- node not responding
- reboot pending
- maintenance
- power state transition
- config mismatch
- manual drain by admin

If you want, I can also explain how `ReqNodeNotAvail` differs from `Resources`, `Priority`, and `QOSMax*` pending reasons.

results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
`ReqNodeNotAvail` is a Slurm pending reason meaning the job is waiting for one or more specifically required nodes, but those nodes are not currently available for scheduling.

Common cases behind it:
- the required node is `DOWN`
- the required node is `DRAIN` or `DRAINING`
- the required node is `FAIL` or `FAILING`
- the node is not responding
- the node is reserved for something else
- the node is rebooting or otherwise temporarily unavailable
- the job requested a specific node or node list, and those exact nodes are busy or unavailable
- a feature/constraint narrows placement to a small set of nodes, and those nodes are unavailable

In practice, this often happens when:
- the user requested `--nodelist`
- the job has constraints like `--constraint`
- a reservation or partition setup limits which nodes can be used
- Slurm knows the needed node exists, but its state prevents allocation

How to distinguish it from other wait reasons:
- `Resources`: suitable resources exist in general, but none are free right now
- `ReqNodeNotAvail`: the job is tied to particular nodes, and those nodes are unavailable

Typical admin/user checks:
- `squeue -j <jobid>` to see the pending reason
- `scontrol show job <jobid>` for more detail on requested nodes/features
- `sinfo -R` to see nodes in down/drain and their reasons
- `sinfo` or `scontrol show node <node>` to inspect node state

Common node availability reasons you may see:
- maintenance
- hardware failure
- not responding
- invalid node configuration
- reboot required
- power issue
- filesystem or network issue
- manually drained by admin
- reserved for another workload

If you want, I can also explain the difference between `ReqNodeNotAvail`, `Resources`, `Priority`, and `BadConstraints`.

results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
`ReqNodeNotAvail` is a Slurm pending reason meaning the job is waiting because the nodes it needs are currently not available for allocation.

Common interpretations:
- the requested node is `DOWN`
- the requested node is `DRAIN`, `DRAINING`, `FAIL`, or `FAILING`
- the node is `FUTURE` and not yet usable
- the node is reserved for something else
- the job requested specific nodes or features and those matching nodes are unavailable
- the node is effectively unavailable because `slurmd` is not responding or the controller marked it unusable

Typical real-world causes behind node unavailability:
- hardware failure
- node reboot or crash
- network/connectivity loss
- `slurmd` stopped or not responding
- admin maintenance drain
- health check failure
- configuration mismatch between node and `slurm.conf`
- insufficient local resources on the node versus configured expectations
- reservation blocking access to the node set

How it differs from simple resource shortage:
- `Resources` usually means suitable nodes exist but are busy
- `ReqNodeNotAvail` usually means the needed node set itself is unavailable, not just occupied

Common availability-related node states to know:
- `DOWN`: not usable; often crashed, unreachable, or manually downed
- `DRAIN`: no new jobs allowed; usually maintenance or problem investigation
- `DRAINING`: finishing current work, then becoming drained
- `FAIL` / `FAILING`: marked bad due to failure conditions
- `FUTURE`: defined but not yet available for scheduling
- reserved nodes: usable only by jobs matching the reservation

Useful admin/user checks:
- `squeue -j <jobid>` to see the pending reason
- `scontrol show job <jobid>` for more detail on requested nodes/features
- `sinfo -R` to see down/drained nodes and reasons
- `scontrol show node <nodename>` to inspect node state and reason
- `scontrol show reservation` to see whether a reservation is blocking access

A very common expanded message is:
- `ReqNodeNotAvail, Reserved for maintenance`
- `ReqNodeNotAvail, UnavailableNodes:<node list>`

That usually tells you whether the block is maintenance/reservation versus specific bad nodes.

results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
`ReqNodeNotAvail` is a Slurm pending reason that means the job is waiting for specific required node(s), but those node(s) are not currently available for allocation.

Typical cases:
- the job explicitly requested certain nodes with `--nodelist` / `-w`
- the job excluded most nodes and only a small required set remains
- the job needs features/resources that currently map to a specific unavailable node set
- the allocated/required nodes are in a non-runnable state

Common node-availability reasons behind `ReqNodeNotAvail`:
- `DOWN`: node is unavailable, often because `slurmd` stopped responding or the node had an error
- `DRAIN` / `DRAINING`: node was administratively removed from service, often for maintenance or hardware/software issues
- `FAIL` / `FAILING`: node is considered unhealthy or failing
- `FUTURE`: node is defined but not yet available for use
- reserved for maintenance or another reservation
- powered down / powering up / reboot pending
- otherwise unavailable due to preserved node state after an issue

How this differs from other pending reasons:
- `Resources`: suitable resources exist in general, but they are busy
- `Priority`: the job is eligible but waiting behind higher-priority jobs
- `ReqNodeNotAvail`: the specific required nodes are unavailable, not merely busy in the normal sense

A practical interpretation:
- if you pinned the job to named hosts, one or more of those hosts is unavailable
- if you did not explicitly name hosts, Slurm may still have reduced the eligible set to unavailable nodes because of constraints, features, reservations, or exclusions

What to check:
- `squeue -j <jobid>` for the pending reason
- `scontrol show job <jobid>` for detailed constraints and requested nodes
- `sinfo -R` to see nodes in down/drain states and their reasons
- `sinfo` to check node states and availability
- reservations/maintenance if the nodes are reserved

Common fixes:
- remove hard node pinning if not required
- relax constraints/features/exclusions
- wait for the node to return to service
- ask admins to inspect drained/down nodes if the job truly requires them

If you want, I can also explain the difference between `ReqNodeNotAvail`, `Resources`, and `Priority` with example `squeue` outputs.

results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
`ReqNodeNotAvail` is a Slurm pending reason meaning the job is waiting because one or more specifically required nodes are not currently available for allocation.

Usually that happens when the job has a hard placement constraint, such as:
- an explicit node request (`--nodelist`, constrained hostlist)
- a reservation or feature constraint that narrows the eligible nodes
- a required node set implied by topology, gres, licenses, or partition limits
- a previous allocation requirement in some workflow setups

Common node-availability causes behind `ReqNodeNotAvail` include:
- `DOWN`: node is unavailable for scheduling
- `DRAIN` / `DRAINED`: node has been taken out of service, often for maintenance or errors
- `FAIL` / `FAILING`: node is unhealthy or being marked failed
- `Not responding`: controller cannot communicate properly with `slurmd` on that node
- `RESERVED`: node is tied up by a reservation your job cannot use
- `ALLOCATED` / busy in practice: the specific required node exists but is not free yet
- `POWERED_DOWN` / power-save related states: node exists but is not immediately usable
- `MAINT` or admin maintenance reason text: node intentionally unavailable
- invalid or impossible constraints: the requested node/feature combination matches nodes that are all unavailable

A useful distinction:
- `Resources` means the cluster could run the job somewhere, just not yet.
- `ReqNodeNotAvail` means the job needs particular nodes, and those nodes are unavailable.

Typical examples:
- You submit with `--nodelist=node05`, but `node05` is drained.
- You request a feature that only exists on two nodes, and both are down.
- Your job is tied to a reservation window or required node set that is not currently usable.

How to investigate:
- Check the queue reason: `squeue`
- Check detailed job constraints: `scontrol show job <jobid>`
- Check node state and reason: `scontrol show node <nodename>` or `sinfo -R`

What to look for in the detailed node reason text:
- hardware or filesystem problems
- `Not responding`
- maintenance notes
- power or reboot transitions
- admin-set drain reasons

In short: `ReqNodeNotAvail` does not usually mean “the cluster is full”; it means “the nodes this job specifically needs are unavailable.”

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol requeue does to a Slurm job
results.agent_response:
`scontrol requeue` tells Slurm to put a job back into the queue to be run again.

In practice, that usually means:

- a running job is terminated and returned to `PENDING`
- a pending job is reset/reinserted for scheduling
- the job keeps the same job ID
- Slurm will try to schedule it again later as a fresh run

Important details:

- It is not the same as `scancel`; the job is not removed, just sent back for rerun.
- Any work not checkpointed or otherwise saved by the application is typically lost.
- Whether requeue is allowed depends on job settings, partition/QOS policy, and permissions.
- For job arrays, requeue can apply to the whole array or specific array elements.
- For heterogeneous jobs, requeue is applied from the leader job and affects all components.

Common use cases:

- retrying a failed or evicted job
- restarting after node problems
- rescheduling work after changing cluster conditions

Typical effect on state:

- `RUNNING` → terminated → `PENDING`
- later, if resources are available, `PENDING` → `RUNNING` again

If you want, I can also explain the difference between `scontrol requeue`, `scontrol hold/release`, and `scancel`.

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol requeue does to a Slurm job
results.agent_response:
`scontrol requeue` takes an existing job and puts it back into the queue to be scheduled again.

In practice, that means:

- a running job is stopped and returned to `PENDING`
- a pending job can be reset and reconsidered by the scheduler
- the job keeps the same job ID
- it is not the same as submitting a brand-new job

Key points:

- It is used to rerun a job from the queue rather than creating a duplicate.
- Whether the job restarts cleanly from the beginning or resumes useful work depends on the application and any checkpoint/restart support.
- Job state/history may reflect that it was requeued.

results.agent_response:
`scontrol requeue` stops a job and puts it back into the queue to be scheduled again.

In practice, that means:

- the job is returned to a pending state
- Slurm will try to run it again later

Whether the job restarts cleanly depends on the application and batch script:
- if the job supports checkpoint/restart, it may continue from saved state
- otherwise it usually starts over from the beginning

So the short version is: `scontrol requeue <jobid>` tells Slurm to take that job and schedule it again as a pending job.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
In Slurm, **hold** and **release** control whether a job is eligible to be scheduled.

- **Hold**
  - A held job stays in the queue but is **not eligible to start**.
  - This is typically applied to a **pending** job.
  - Conceptually, the job is blocked from normal scheduling until someone removes the hold.
  - Users can generally hold their own jobs, subject to site policy; privileged users can act more broadly.

- **Release**
  - Releasing a held job makes it **eligible for scheduling again**.
  - The job returns to normal pending behavior and can start when resources and policy allow.

Key practical points:

- A hold does **not cancel** the job.
- A hold does **not remove** the job from the queue.
- Release does **not force immediate start**; it only restores eligibility.
- Eligibility after release still depends on normal scheduling factors like:
  - priority
  - fairshare
  - partition/QOS limits
  - dependencies
  - resource availability

Common admin/user commands are:

- `scontrol hold <jobid>`
- `scontrol release <jobid>`

Related semantics:

- If a job is pending for another reason, releasing it only removes the **hold** aspect; other blockers can still keep it pending.
- For active/running jobs, hold/release is generally about queued eligibility semantics rather than stopping a running job.

If you want, I can also explain the difference between **user holds**, **admin holds**, and how they appear in job reason/status fields.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
In Slurm, a job hold means the job is kept from starting even if resources are otherwise available. A release removes that hold so the job can compete for scheduling again.

Key semantics:

- Hold applies to pending jobs.
- A held job stays in the queue, but Slurm will not start it.
- Release only removes the hold; it does not force immediate start.

Common behavior:
- `scontrol hold <jobid>` places a hold on a job.
- `scontrol release <jobid>` removes that hold.
- After release, the job returns to normal pending scheduling behavior and waits according to priority, limits, dependencies, reservations, resources, and policy.

Important nuances:
- A released job is not guaranteed to run right away.
- If the job still has another blocker, it remains pending for that reason.
- Holds are distinct from suspend/resume:
  - hold/release affects whether a pending job may start
  - suspend/resume affects a running job

Permissions:
- Users can generally hold and release their own jobs, subject to site policy and Slurm permissions.
- Privileged users/admins can do so for other users’ jobs.

Related detail from Slurm docs:
- Slurm also documents an alternate “hold-like” mechanism by pushing a job’s `StartTime` into the future, then resetting it later. That prevents initiation, but it is different from the explicit hold/release commands.

For arrays:
- Holding an array parent job ID can affect all elements.
- Individual array tasks can also be targeted using `ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID` notation.

Practical effect in queue state:
- A held job usually appears as pending with a hold-related reason/state indicator, depending on site configuration and command output format.
- Once released, the pending reason changes back to whatever scheduling condition applies.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
In Slurm, hold/release controls whether a job is eligible to be scheduled.

- Hold:
  - A held job stays in `PENDING`.
  - It is intentionally blocked from starting.
  - Slurm typically shows a pending reason indicating the hold, commonly user-hold or admin-hold semantics.
  - A held job is not considered normally schedulable until the hold is removed.

- Release:
  - Releasing removes that scheduling block.
  - The job remains `PENDING` if resources are still not available, but it becomes eligible to run again.
  - After release, its pending reason may change from a hold-related reason to the normal scheduling reason, such as waiting for resources, priority, dependency, or limits.

Common semantics:

- User hold vs admin hold:
  - User-originated holds and administrator-originated holds are distinct in Slurm state/reason reporting.
  - In practice, this lets Slurm record whether the job was blocked by the user or by an admin action.

- Priority interaction:
  - While held, the job is not eligible for dispatch.
  - Releasing the job makes it eligible again; scheduling then follows normal priority, partition, QOS, dependency, and resource rules.

- Scope:
  - Hold/release is mainly meaningful for pending jobs.
  - It is used to pause future start, not to stop a job that is already running.

Typical commands:

- Hold a job:
  - `scontrol hold <jobid>`
- Release a job:
  - `scontrol release <jobid>`

Operationally:

- If a job is pending because it is held, release does not force immediate start.
- Release only removes the hold condition.
- If other blockers remain, the job still waits in queue.

Related distinction:

- `hold/release` affects scheduling eligibility.
- `suspend/resume` affects an already running job.
- `cancel` terminates a job instead of pausing its eligibility.

If you want, I can also explain how hold/release differs from dependency blocking, priority aging, and `BeginTime`.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
In Slurm, a held job is a job that is prevented from being scheduled until the hold is removed.

Basics:
- `scontrol hold <jobid>` places a hold on a pending job.
- `scontrol release <jobid>` removes that hold.

What hold does:
- It keeps the job in the queue, but not eligible to start.
- Practically, Slurm treats the job as not runnable until released.
- A held job is typically shown as pending with a hold-related reason, and its effective scheduling priority is suppressed while held.

Common semantics:
- Hold applies to jobs that are still pending. It is not a general-purpose pause for a running job.
- Releasing the job does not force it to start immediately; it only makes it eligible again. After release, normal scheduling rules apply:
  - partition limits
  - QOS/account limits
  - dependencies
  - fairshare/priority
  - resource availability

User vs admin hold:
- A regular user can generally hold and release their own jobs, subject to site policy.
- Administrators can hold/release any job.
- Some sites distinguish user hold vs admin hold behavior in tooling or reason strings, but the core effect is the same: the job stays pending and unschedulable until the relevant hold is cleared.

Interaction with dependencies and priority:
- Holding a job is separate from dependencies.
- If you release a job that still has an unmet dependency, it will remain pending for the dependency reason.
- After release, the job re-enters normal priority-based scheduling; release does not guarantee preserved queue position in any special sense beyond whatever Slurm’s priority system computes.

Arrays and heterogeneous jobs:
- For job arrays, hold/release can be applied to the whole array or specific elements depending on how the job ID is specified.
- Site/version behavior can differ slightly in presentation, but the scheduling meaning is the same.

Related but different actions:
- `scontrol suspend` / `resume` affect running jobs, not pending eligibility in the same way.
- `scancel` removes the job entirely.
- `scontrol requeue` sends a job back to pending state; it is not the same as holding it.

A simple mental model:
- hold = “keep this pending job from starting”
- release = “allow this pending job to compete for scheduling again”

results.prompt: Explain how scancel sends signals to jobs and steps
results.agent_response:
`scancel` can either:

- cancel a whole job,
- signal a whole job allocation,
- or signal/cancel individual job steps.

Key behavior from Slurm docs:

- `scancel JOBID` with no `--signal` cancels the entire job.
- `scancel --signal=... JOBID` sends a signal to the job’s steps, but does not behave the same as a full cancel.
- `scancel JOBID.STEPID` targets a specific step.

How signals are delivered:

- Full job cancel: `scancel JOBID`
  - Slurm sends `SIGCONT` to all steps first,
  - then `SIGTERM`,
  - waits `KillWait`,
  - then sends `SIGKILL` if anything is still alive.
  - This is the normal termination path for a job.

- Signal a job allocation: `scancel --signal=TERM JOBID`
  - All job steps are signaled.
  - The batch script itself is not signaled unless `--batch` is used.
  - This does not necessarily cancel the job in the same sense as plain `scancel JOBID`.

- Signal only the batch shell: `scancel --signal=USR1 --batch JOBID`
  - Only the batch step (the shell running the script) is signaled.
  - Child processes are not directly signaled by Slurm.
  - The shell may trap/forward the signal itself.

- Signal specific steps: `scancel --signal=TERM JOBID.STEPID`
  - Only those named steps are signaled.
  - Cancelling a step does not terminate the whole job allocation.

Important nuance:

- By default, signals other than `SIGKILL` are not sent to the batch step unless `--batch` is used.
- If you send `KILL` to an entire job with `--signal=KILL`, Slurm kills the active steps but does not cancel the job itself the same way plain `scancel JOBID` does.
- For scripts, trapping a signal in the batch shell can be useful, but many shells will not process the signal until the foreground child command exits.

Examples:

- Cancel whole job:
  - `scancel 1234`

- Send `SIGTERM` to steps 1 and 3 only:
  - `scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 1234.3`

- Send `SIGUSR1` to the batch shell only:
  - `scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236`

- Send `SIGKILL` to all steps, without normal cancel flow:
  - `scancel --signal=KILL 1235`

In short: plain `scancel JOBID` is a structured cancel sequence for the whole job; `--signal` is for explicit signal delivery, usually to steps, and `--batch` changes that target to the batch shell.

results.prompt: Compare srun, sbatch, and salloc from the Slurm docs
results.agent_response:
From the Slurm docs:

- `sbatch`: submits a batch script to Slurm. It “exits immediately after the script is successfully transferred to the Slurm controller and assigned a Slurm job ID,” and the job may remain pending before resources are granted.
- `salloc`: obtains a job allocation first, then runs a user command in that allocation; if no command is given, it runs the user’s default shell. When that command exits, the allocation is relinquished.
- `srun`: runs a parallel job. If needed, it “will first create a resource allocation in which to run the parallel job.”

Practical comparison:

- `sbatch` = non-interactive batch submission
  - Best for scripts and queued workloads
  - Typical use: `sbatch train.sh`
  - The script can contain `#SBATCH` directives

- `salloc` = interactive allocation
  - Best when you want reserved resources and then an interactive shell or command
  - Typical use: `salloc -N2 bash`
  - Common pattern from docs: get an allocation, then run `srun` inside it

- `srun` = launch work, often parallel tasks
  - Best for starting tasks directly, either inside an existing allocation or by creating one if necessary
  - Typical use: `srun -n8 hostname`
  - Often used inside `sbatch` scripts and inside `salloc` sessions for job steps

Rule of thumb:

- Use `sbatch` for scheduled batch jobs
- Use `salloc` for interactive sessions
- Use `srun` to launch the actual program/tasks

One subtle point from the docs: `srun` can create an allocation itself, but `salloc` is specifically focused on acquiring an allocation and then letting you work interactively within it.

Signals sent to the srun command are automatically forwarded to
the tasks it is controlling with a few exceptions. The escape sequence
<control-c> will report the state of all tasks associated with
the srun command. If <control-c> is entered twice within
one second, then the associated SIGINT signal will be sent to all tasks
and a termination sequence will be entered sending SIGCONT, SIGTERM,
and SIGKILL to all spawned tasks.

terminated without waiting for remote tasks to exit or their I/O to
complete.

From the Slurm docs:

- `sbatch`: submits a batch script to Slurm and returns immediately after the job is accepted and assigned a job ID. The script may wait in the queue before resources are granted. It is for non-interactive batch jobs.

Docs-backed examples:
- `sbatch myscript` submits a script containing `#SBATCH` directives and often `srun ...` inside it.
- `salloc -N5 srun -n10 myprogram` gets resources, then runs the program.
- `salloc -N16 xterm` or just `salloc` gives an interactive environment after allocation.

A simple mental model:
- `sbatch` = submit batch job
- `salloc` = get interactive allocation
- `srun` = run tasks/job steps

results.agent_response:
`sattach` is used to attach to a running Slurm job step.

What it does:
- connects to an already running step of a job
- exposes the step’s I/O streams, so you can see task output/error interactively

- it cannot attach directly to `batch` or `extern` steps, because those I/O channels are not directly forwarded the same way

- that created a running step
- you use `sattach <jobid.stepid>` to reconnect to that step’s I/O/debug context

It’s basically a “reattach to a running step” tool, whereas:
- `srun` starts a step
- `salloc` gets an allocation
- `sbatch` submits a batch job
- `sattach` reconnects to an existing running step

One caution from the Slurm docs: `sattach` sends RPCs to `slurmctld`, so it should not be called repeatedly in loops.

results.prompt: Explain sbcast and when it helps stage files to allocated nodes
results.agent_response:
`sbcast` is Slurm’s file-broadcast command. It copies a file from the current node to all nodes allocated to the current job.

When it helps:
- You have a job allocation already.
- The destination should be on node-local storage.
- You want the same file on every allocated node without each node pulling it separately.
- Typical use: stage an executable, model file, config, or input bundle onto local disk before launching tasks.

When it is most useful:
- To avoid many nodes hammering a shared filesystem for the same file.
- To place files on faster local storage on compute nodes.
- For startup staging inside a batch job or interactive allocation.

Important limits from Slurm docs:
- It should be run only from within a Slurm batch job or from a shell inside an active allocation.
- The destination should be a fully qualified path and should be on a filesystem local to the node.
- Parallel filesystems may sometimes perform better than `sbcast`; it depends on file size, parallelism, and network.
- Don’t call `sbcast` repeatedly in loops, because it sends RPCs to `slurmctld` and can hurt controller performance.

In short: use `sbcast` when you already have nodes allocated and want to efficiently stage the same file onto each allocated node’s local storage, especially to reduce shared-filesystem pressure.

- If the file already lives on a high-performance parallel filesystem and nodes can read it efficiently there.

- If you need to broadcast many files by calling `sbcast` repeatedly in a loop.
- If the destination is not node-local, since the docs note parallel filesystems may perform better depending on file size, parallelism, and network.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm GRES syntax and gpu resource requests
results.agent_response:
In Slurm, GPUs are usually requested as a kind of GRES: Generic RESource.

Core syntax:
- `--gres=name[:type:count]`
- For GPUs, that is commonly:
  - `--gres=gpu:1`
  - `--gres=gpu:a100:2`

From the docs:
- `--gres` means generic resources required per node
- `--gpus` means GPUs required per job
- `--gpus-per-node` means GPUs required per node
- `--gpus-per-node` is equivalent to `--gres` for GPUs
- `--gpus-per-socket` and `--gpus-per-task` are also supported
- The `--gpu*` options are supported only with Slurm’s `select/cons_tres` plugin

Practical meanings:
- `--gres=gpu:2`
  - request 2 GPUs per node
- `--gres=gpu:a100:2`
  - request 2 GPUs of type `a100` per node
- `--gpus=2`
  - request 2 GPUs total for the job
- `--gpus-per-node=2`
  - request 2 GPUs on each allocated node
- `--gpus-per-task=1`
  - request 1 GPU per task, so task count matters

Common examples:

Batch job:
```bash
sbatch --gres=gpu:1 job.sh
```

Typed GPU request:
```bash
sbatch --gres=gpu:v100:2 job.sh
```

Using the newer GPU flags:
```bash
sbatch --gpus=4 job.sh
sbatch --gpus-per-node=2 --nodes=2 job.sh
sbatch --ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1 job.sh
```

Equivalent forms for per-node GPU requests:
```bash
sbatch --gres=gpu:2 job.sh
sbatch --gpus-per-node=2 job.sh
```

How to choose:
- Use `--gres=gpu[:type]:count` when you want explicit GRES syntax, especially with GPU type
- Use `--gpus` when you care about total GPUs for the whole job
- Use `--gpus-per-node` when every allocated node must have that many GPUs
- Use `--gpus-per-task` when each task/process needs its own GPU

Important caveats:
- `--gres` is per node
- `--gpus` is per job
- If you request a GPU type, the type string must match what the cluster configured
- If the cluster does not use `select/cons_tres`, `--gpus*` options may be rejected, while `--gres` is the traditional form

Typical combinations:
```bash
sbatch -N1 -n4 --gpus-per-task=1 job.sh
```
This means 4 tasks and 1 GPU per task.

```bash
sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=4 job.sh
```
This means 2 nodes, 4 GPUs on each node.

```bash
sbatch -N1 --gres=gpu:a100:2 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=64G job.sh
```
This means 1 node with 2 A100 GPUs, plus CPU and memory requirements.

Inside a batch script, the same can be written as directives:
```bash
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:2

results.prompt: Explain Slurm GRES syntax and gpu resource requests
results.agent_response:
In Slurm, GPUs are usually requested as **GRES**: generic resources.

## Core GRES syntax

The general form is:

```bash
--gres=name[:type:count]
```

For GPUs, that usually means:

```bash
--gres=gpu[:type:count]
```

Examples:

```bash
--gres=gpu:1
--gres=gpu:4
--gres=gpu:a100:2
```

Meaning:
- `gpu` = request GPU resources
- `a100` = request a specific GPU type, if configured that way on the cluster
- `2` = number requested

From Slurm docs, jobs are not allocated GRES unless explicitly requested, and `--gres` is supported by `sbatch`, `srun`, and `salloc`.

## GPU-specific request options

Slurm also supports GPU-focused flags:

- `--gpus` = GPUs required per job
- `--gpus-per-node` = GPUs required per node
- `--gpus-per-socket` = GPUs required per socket
- `--gpus-per-task` = GPUs required per task

Docs note:
- `--gpus-per-node` is equivalent to `--gres` for GPUs
- `--gpus-per-task` requires a task count
- `--gpus-per-socket` requires socket-aware task placement
- the `--gpu*` options require the `select/cons_tres` plugin

## Common patterns

### 1 GPU total
```bash
sbatch --gpus=1 job.sh
```

or

```bash
sbatch --gres=gpu:1 job.sh
```

### 2 GPUs of a specific type
```bash
sbatch --gres=gpu:a100:2 job.sh
```

### 4 GPUs on each node
```bash
sbatch --nodes=2 --gpus-per-node=4 job.sh
```

### 1 GPU per task
```bash
sbatch --ntasks=8 --gpus-per-task=1 job.sh
```

This is often used for multi-process training.

## Difference between `--gres=gpu:N` and `--gpus=N`

In many clusters they behave similarly for ordinary GPU requests, but:
- `--gres` is the more general GRES mechanism
- `--gpus*` is the GPU-specific interface
- clusters may expose GPU **types** through GRES naming, so `--gres=gpu:a100:2` is a common typed request form

## Typed GPUs

If admins configured GPU types, you can request a specific model:

```bash
--gres=gpu:v100:1
--gres=gpu:a100:4
```

The exact type string must match the cluster’s configured GPU type name.

## Multi-node semantics

Be careful with scope:
- `--gpus=4` = 4 GPUs for the whole job
- `--gpus-per-node=4` = 4 GPUs on each allocated node
- `--gres=gpu:4` is generally per node in Slurm’s GRES syntax

That per-node behavior is a common source of confusion.

## Typical batch script example

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=train
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00

python train.py
```

Typed GPU example:

```bash
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:a100:2
```

## With `srun`

Interactive or step-level GPU request:

```bash
srun --gres=gpu:1 python train.py
```

or

```bash
srun --ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1 python distributed.py
```

## Important practical notes

- GPU requests only work if the cluster has GPUs configured in Slurm.
- Typed requests only work if GPU types were configured.
- `--gpus*` options may be rejected if the cluster is not using `select/cons_tres`.
- Requesting GPUs does not automatically set CPU, memory, or task layout correctly; you usually also want `--cpus-per-task`, `--mem`, and possibly `--ntasks`.

## Rule of thumb

Use:
- `--gres=gpu:1` for simple, portable single-node GPU requests
- `--gres=gpu:<type>:N` when you need a specific GPU model
- `--gpus-per-task=1` for distributed jobs with one GPU per rank/task
- `--gpus-per-node=N` when you care about per-node GPU count explicitly

If you want, I can also explain:
1. **`--gres` vs `--tres-per-task`**
2. **how GPU requests interact with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`**
3. **how to write correct multi-GPU Slurm scripts**

results.prompt: Explain Slurm GRES syntax and gpu resource requests
results.agent_response:
In Slurm, GPUs are usually requested as a kind of GRES: Generic RESource.

Core syntax:
- `--gres=name[:type:count]`
- For GPUs, that is typically:
  - `--gres=gpu:1`
  - `--gres=gpu:4`
  - `--gres=gpu:a100:2`

Meaning:
- `name` = resource family, usually `gpu`
- `type` = optional model/type configured by the cluster, such as `a100`, `v100`, `rtx6000`
- `count` = how many of that resource you want

Examples:
- 1 GPU of any type:
  - `sbatch --gres=gpu:1 job.sh`
- 2 A100 GPUs per node:
  - `sbatch --gres=gpu:a100:2 job.sh`
- Interactive job with 1 GPU:
  - `srun --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash`

Slurm also supports GPU-specific options:
- `--gpus=<count>` → GPUs required per job
- `--gpus-per-node=<count>` → GPUs per node
- `--gpus-per-task=<count>` → GPUs per task
- `--gpus-per-socket=<count>` → GPUs per socket

From the docs:
- `--gpus-per-node` is equivalent to `--gres` for GPUs
- These GPU-specific options are supported by `salloc`, `sbatch`, and `srun`
- They require the `select/cons_tres` plugin to be configured

Typical examples:
- Total 2 GPUs for the job:
  - `sbatch --gpus=2 job.sh`
- 1 GPU on each allocated node:
  - `sbatch --nodes=2 --gpus-per-node=1 job.sh`
- 1 GPU per task for 4 tasks:
  - `sbatch --ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1 job.sh`

Important distinction:
- `--gres=gpu:2` is node-oriented: request 2 GPUs on each allocated node
- `--gpus=2` is job-oriented: request 2 GPUs for the whole job

Type-qualified requests:
- `--gres=gpu:a100:2` requests a specific GPU type
- The type string must match what the cluster configured in Slurm

Multiple GRES can be combined:
- Example syntax from the docs/design guide:
  - `"gpu:2,nic:1"`
So a job may request several generic resources together, depending on site configuration.

Common patterns in batch scripts:
```bash
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
```

Or with typed GPUs:
```bash
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:a100:2
```

A few practical notes:
- Requesting a GPU does not automatically choose CPUs or memory appropriately; you often also set `--cpus-per-task`, `--mem`, and `--time`
- GPU type names are cluster-specific
- If a cluster is not configured for the GPU-specific `--gpus*` options, those requests can be rejected
- Jobs get no GRES unless they explicitly request them

Rule of thumb:
- Use `--gres=gpu[:type]:count` when you want explicit GRES syntax or a typed GPU
- Use `--gpus*` when you want job-, node-, or task-oriented GPU requests in a more expressive form

If you want, I can also explain:
- the difference between `--gres=gpu:2` and `--gpus-per-task=1`
- how GPU requests interact with `--ntasks`, `--nodes`, and `--cpus-per-task`
- how to write correct GPU `sbatch` headers for single-node vs multi-node jobs

results.prompt: Explain --gres=gpu:N and GPU allocation behavior
results.agent_response:
`--gres=gpu:N` requests `N` GPU generic resources per node.

Key behavior:
- `--gres` syntax is `name[:type:count]`
- So:
  - `--gres=gpu:1` = request 1 GPU on each allocated node
  - `--gres=gpu:4` = request 4 GPUs on each allocated node
  - `--gres=gpu:a100:2` = request 2 GPUs of type `a100` per node, if types are configured

Important allocation semantics:
- Slurm does not allocate GPUs unless you explicitly request them with `--gres`, `--gpus`, or related `--gpus-*` options.
- `--gres=gpu:N` is per-node, not per-job.
- If your job gets multiple nodes, each node must satisfy that GPU count.

Examples:
- `sbatch --gres=gpu:2 job.sh`
  - one-node job requesting 2 GPUs on that node
- `sbatch -N 3 --gres=gpu:2 job.sh`
  - three nodes, 2 GPUs on each node, total 6 GPUs

Related options:
- `--gpus=X` = GPUs required per job
- `--gpus-per-node=X` = equivalent to GPU `--gres` per node
- `--gpus-per-task=X` = GPUs per task
- `--gpus-per-socket=X` = GPUs per socket

Runtime behavior:
- Slurm tracks those GPUs as allocated to the job.
- Steps launched inside the job can inherit or further constrain GPU visibility depending on site config and step options.
- In many configurations, Slurm limits visibility with environment variables like `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, so the job sees only its assigned GPUs.

A few practical gotchas:
- `--gres=gpu:N` alone does not say how many CPUs or tasks you want.
- GPU count and task layout are separate, so you often also specify things like:
  - `--ntasks`
  - `--cpus-per-task`
  - `--mem`
- If you want one GPU per task, `--gpus-per-task=1` is often clearer than only using `--gres=gpu:N`.

Common confusion:
- `--gres=gpu:4` does not necessarily mean “4 GPUs total” unless the job uses one node.
- For multi-node jobs, total GPUs = GPUs per node × allocated nodes.
- GPU type requests only work if the cluster defines typed GPU GRES.

Typical patterns:
- Single-node training:
  - `sbatch --gres=gpu:4 --cpus-per-task=8 job.sh`
- Distributed multi-node:
  - `sbatch -N 2 --ntasks-per-node=4 --gpus-per-node=4 job.sh`
- Typed GPU request:
  - `sbatch --gres=gpu:a100:2 job.sh`

If you want, I can also explain how `--gres=gpu:N` differs from `--gpus`, `--gpus-per-task`, and `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` in practice.

results.prompt: Explain --gres=gpu:N and GPU allocation behavior
results.agent_response:
`--gres=gpu:N` requests `N` GPU generic resources per node.

Key points:

- `--gres` syntax is `name[:type:count]`
- For GPUs, `--gres=gpu:N` means:
  - allocate `N` GPUs
  - on each allocated node where that request applies

Typical behavior:

- `sbatch --gres=gpu:2 ...`
  - asks for 2 GPUs on the job allocation node(s)
- `srun --gres=gpu:1 ...`
  - asks for 1 GPU for that step
- `--gpus-per-node=N` is documented as equivalent to `--gres=gpu:N`

Important allocation behavior from Slurm docs:

- Jobs are not given GPUs unless they explicitly request them.
- GPU requests are supported by `salloc`, `sbatch`, and `srun`.
- The `--gpu*` options require the `select/cons_tres` plugin.
- Slurm can expose the assigned devices through `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`.

How this usually plays out:

1. At submit time
   - Slurm sees the job needs GPUs.
   - The job only becomes eligible for nodes with enough configured free GPU GRES.

2. At allocation time
   - Slurm reserves the requested number of GPUs for the job.
   - If configured with device isolation/cgroups, the job sees only its assigned GPU device files.

3. Inside the job
   - `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` is typically set to the GPUs assigned to that job or step.
   - The visible numbering may be remapped relative to the physical GPU IDs.

Common distinctions:

- `--gres=gpu:N`
  - request GPUs as a generic resource
- `--gpus=N`
  - request GPUs per job
- `--gpus-per-node=N`
  - GPUs per node
- `--gpus-per-task=N`
  - GPUs per task, requires task count context

Practical examples:

- One-node job needing 2 GPUs:
  - `sbatch --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:2 job.sh`
- Two-node job needing 1 GPU on each node:
  - `sbatch --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:1 job.sh`
- Four tasks, one GPU per task:
  - usually use `--ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1`

Subtleties to watch for:

- `--gres=gpu:N` is per node, not automatically “total across all nodes”.
- If you ask for multiple nodes, Slurm interprets the GRES request in the node context.
- A job allocation and an `srun` step can have different GPU requests; step-level requests subdivide what the allocation has available.
- Type-specific requests are possible, e.g. `--gres=gpu:a100:2`, if the cluster defines GPU types.

Also, requesting GPUs does not by itself define:

- how many CPUs you get
- how many tasks run
- which task uses which GPU

Those are influenced by options like:

- `--cpus-per-task`
- `--ntasks`
- `--nodes`
- `--ntasks-per-node`
- `--gpu-bind` or site-specific policies

If you want, I can also explain the difference between `--gres=gpu:N`, `--gpus=N`, and `--gpus-per-task=N` with concrete multi-node examples.

results.prompt: Explain --gres=gpu:N and GPU allocation behavior
results.agent_response:
`--gres=gpu:N` means: request `N` GPU generic resources per allocated node.

Key behavior:

- `--gres` syntax is `name[:type:count]`
- For GPUs, common forms are:
  - `--gres=gpu:2` → 2 GPUs per node
  - `--gres=gpu:a100:2` → 2 GPUs of type `a100` per node

What Slurm does:

- Slurm does not allocate GPUs unless you explicitly request them with `--gres`, `--gpus`, `--gpus-per-node`, `--gpus-per-task`, or similar.
- With `--gres=gpu:N`, each allocated node must provide `N` GPUs.
- If your job gets multiple nodes, the request applies to each node, not the whole job.

Examples:

- `sbatch --gres=gpu:1 job.sh`
  - one node with 1 GPU
- `sbatch -N2 --gres=gpu:2 job.sh`
  - two nodes, each with 2 GPUs, so 4 GPUs total

Related options:

- `--gpus=X` → GPUs required for the whole job
- `--gpus-per-node=X` → equivalent in intent to `--gres=gpu:X` for GPUs
- `--gpus-per-task=X` → GPUs tied to task count
- `--gpus-per-socket=X` → GPUs tied to sockets

Allocation details:

- Slurm allocates GPU resources at scheduling time based on configured GRES on the node.
- The exact GPU devices assigned are exposed to the job environment, typically through `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`.
- A job can only use the GPUs it was allocated.
- GPU requests are independent from CPU and memory requests, so you usually also want to request CPUs and memory explicitly.

Important nuance:

- `--gres=gpu:N` is per node, not per job.
- If you need exactly 2 GPUs total and don’t want that interpreted per node across multiple nodes, use options consistent with your node count and task layout.

Typed GPUs:

- If the cluster defines GPU types, you can request a specific type with `--gres=gpu:type:N`.
- If types are not configured in Slurm, type-specific requests will not work.

Scheduling consequences:

- Your job remains pending until nodes exist that satisfy all requested resources together:
  - GPUs
  - CPUs
  - memory
  - time limit
  - partition/QOS/account constraints

In practice:

- `--gres=gpu:N` reserves the GPUs for your job on each allocated node.
- It does not automatically guarantee your application will use them correctly; your launcher and software still need to respect the assigned devices.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm --constraint syntax for node features
results.agent_response:
In Slurm, `--constraint` matches node feature labels. You use it with `sbatch`, `srun`, or `salloc` to require nodes with specific features.

Basic form:
- `--constraint=feature`
- Example: `--constraint=gpu`

Common syntax:

- Single feature:
  - `--constraint=amd`
  - Node must have feature `amd`.

- AND:
  - `--constraint="amd&infiniband"`
  - Node must have both features.

- OR:
  - `--constraint="amd|intel"`
  - Node may have either feature.

- Multiple features with brackets for matching sets:
  - `--constraint="[rack1|rack2]"`
  - One of those grouped options must match.
  - Brackets matter when combining expressions.

- Counts with feature multiplicity:
  - `--constraint="graphics*4"`
  - Request nodes with that feature count semantics where supported by Slurm’s feature handling.

- Matching OR groups plus AND:
  - `--constraint="[a|b]&gpu"`
  - Must have `gpu` and also either `a` or `b`.

- Parenthesized-style grouping is generally done with square brackets in Slurm constraint expressions, not shell-style parentheses.

Important behavior:
- Features are administrator-defined node labels.
- The exact feature names available depend on the cluster configuration.
- `--constraint` filters eligible nodes; it does not itself request GPUs, CPUs, or memory. Those are separate options like `--gpus`, `--cpus-per-task`, `--mem`.

Examples:
- `sbatch --constraint=zen4 job.sh`
- `srun --constraint="ssd&avx512" hostname`
- `sbatch --constraint="[a100|h100]&nvme" train.sh`

Related option:
- `--prefer=feature_expr`
  - Expresses a preference rather than a hard requirement.

One practical caution:
- Quote expressions containing `&`, `|`, or brackets so the shell does not interpret them.

If you want, I can also explain the difference between `--constraint`, `--batch`, node features, and GRES like `--gpus`.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm --constraint syntax for node features
results.agent_response:
`--constraint` matches node feature tags configured by the cluster, and the syntax lets you combine them with logical expressions.

Common forms:

- Single feature  
  `--constraint=gpu`
  - Node must have feature `gpu`.

- AND  
  `--constraint="gpu&nvme"`
  - Node must have both `gpu` and `nvme`.

- OR  
  `--constraint="a|b"`
  - Node may have `a` or `b`.

- Parentheses for grouping  
  `--constraint="(a|b)&c"`
  - Node must have `c` and also either `a` or `b`.

- Matching OR across all allocated nodes  
  `--constraint="[a|b]"`
  - Allocation must use nodes that all satisfy the same choice, either all `a` or all `b`.
  - Without brackets, different nodes in the allocation can satisfy different sides of the OR.

- Multiple-count syntax  
  `--constraint="[rack1*2&rack2*4]"`
  - Request specific counts of nodes with given features in one allocation expression.
  - Exact support can depend on the Slurm feature configuration and version.

Important distinction:

- `a|b` means per-node OR.
- `[a|b]` means matching OR: all allocated nodes must use the same branch.

Examples:

- Any GPU node with IB:  
  `sbatch --constraint="gpu&ib" job.sh`

- Either AMD or Intel nodes, but all nodes in the job must be the same type:  
  `sbatch --nodes=4 --constraint="[amd|intel]" job.sh`

- Nodes with SSD plus either AVX2 or AVX512:  
  `srun --constraint="ssd&(avx2|avx512)" ...`

Notes:

- Feature names are cluster-defined. `gpu`, `amd`, `nvme`, etc. only work if your admins configured those exact node features.
- `--constraint` applies to node features, not generic resources like GPU count. For GPU quantity, use options like `--gpus`, `--gres`, or related resource flags.
- Shell quoting is recommended whenever you use `&`, `|`, or parentheses.

If you want, I can also explain the difference between `--constraint`, `--gres`, and `--prefer`.

results.agent_response:
In Slurm, `--constraint` matches node feature labels. You use it in `sbatch`, `salloc`, or `srun` to require nodes with specific features.

Basic forms:

- Single feature:
  - `--constraint=gpu`
  - node must have feature `gpu`

- AND:
  - `--constraint="gpu&nvme"`
  - node must have both `gpu` and `nvme`

- OR:
  - `--constraint="zen4|icelake"`
  - node may have either feature

- Grouping:
  - `--constraint="gpu&(a100|h100)"`
  - node must have `gpu` and either `a100` or `h100`

Common syntax rules:

- `&` = logical AND
- `|` = logical OR
- parentheses `(...)` group expressions
- quote the expression to protect shell metacharacters, especially with `&` and `|`

Examples:

- `sbatch --constraint="avx512" job.sh`
- `srun --constraint="ssd&ib" -N2 hostname`
- `salloc --constraint="(epyc|xeon)&gpu" -N1`

Important behavior:

- Constraints apply to node features configured in Slurm, not arbitrary hardware detection.
- Feature names are site-defined, so `gpu`, `a100`, `amd`, `omnipath`, etc. only work if your cluster admin configured them as node features.
- For multi-node jobs, Slurm tries to satisfy the constraint for all allocated nodes unless the site uses more advanced feature plugins/configuration.

Related option:

- `--prefer=feature_expr`
  - expresses preference rather than a hard requirement
  - example: `--prefer="nvme"` prefers NVMe nodes, but can run elsewhere if needed

How to see available features:

- Users typically inspect node info with:
  - `sinfo -o "%P %N %f"`
  - or `scontrol show node <node>`

Practical examples:

- Require A100 nodes:
  - `sbatch --constraint="a100" train.sh`

- Require GPU nodes with local SSD:
  - `sbatch --constraint="gpu&nvme" train.sh`

- Accept either Milan or Genoa CPU nodes:
  - `sbatch --constraint="milan|genoa" job.sh`

- Require Infiniband plus one of two GPU types:
  - `sbatch --constraint="ib&(v100|a100)" train.sh`

If you want, I can also explain:
- feature counts like bracketed matching syntax if your site uses them,

results.prompt: Explain Slurm --constraint syntax for node features
results.agent_response:
Slurm `--constraint` matches node feature labels, and the syntax is basically boolean logic over those features.

Common forms:

- Single feature:
  - `--constraint=gpu`
  - Node must have feature `gpu`

- AND:
  - `--constraint="gpu&nvme"`
  - Node must have both `gpu` and `nvme`

- OR:
  - `--constraint="zen4|icelake"`
  - Node may have either feature

- Grouping:
  - `--constraint="gpu&(nvme|ssd)"`
  - Requires `gpu` and also one of `nvme` or `ssd`

- Matching OR across all allocated nodes:
  - `--constraint="[rack1|rack2]"`
  - All nodes in the allocation must satisfy the same choice from that bracketed OR set, rather than mixing `rack1` and `rack2`
  - Without brackets, Slurm may mix nodes matching different sides of the OR

- Multiple-count feature requests:
  - `--constraint="graphics*4"`
  - Means a request involving feature counts across nodes, when that feature model is configured by the site
  - Availability and exact behavior depend on how node features are defined locally

Important points:

- Feature names come from the cluster’s node `AvailableFeatures` / configured node features.
- `&` means logical AND, `|` means logical OR.
- Parentheses control precedence.
- Quote the expression so the shell does not interpret `&`, `|`, or parentheses.
- `--constraint` is about node features, not generic resources like CPUs, memory, or GPUs counts. Those usually use options like `--cpus-per-task`, `--mem`, `--gres=gpu:...`.

Examples:

- Batch:
  - `sbatch --constraint="gpu&ib" job.sh`

- Interactive:
  - `srun --constraint="zen4|milan" --pty bash`

- Mixed logic:
  - `sbatch --constraint="a100&(nvlink|pcie4)" train.sh`

One subtlety: exact supported expressions can depend on Slurm version and whether the site uses standard features or helpers like NodeFeatures plugins. If you want, I can also summarize the official precedence and the square-bracket “matching OR” behavior in more detail.

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Node features are labels attached to nodes that Slurm can use as placement constraints.

How they affect placement:
- If you request a feature, Slurm only considers nodes that advertise that feature.
- This is commonly done with `--constraint` in `sbatch`, `srun`, or `salloc`.
- Fewer eligible nodes usually means longer queue time, because the scheduler has a smaller placement pool.

Typical examples:
- Hardware type: `gpu`, `a100`, `infiniband`
- CPU/vendor/gen: `amd`, `intel`, `zen4`
- Storage/local resources: `nvme`, `ssd`
- Site-defined roles/capabilities: `highmem`, `debug`, `avx512`

Basic effect:
- No constraint: job can land on any node that fits requested resources.
- With `--constraint=gpu`: job can land only on nodes with feature `gpu`.
- With multiple feature logic, placement narrows or broadens depending on the expression.

Common constraint behavior:
- `--constraint=foo`  
  Require feature `foo`.
- `--constraint="foo&bar"`  
  Require both `foo` and `bar` on the same eligible node set.
- `--constraint="foo|bar"`  
  Accept either `foo` or `bar`.
- Parentheses can group expressions.

Why this matters:
- Features are filters, not resources by themselves.
- Asking for `--constraint=a100` does not automatically request a GPU count; you often still need resource options like `--gpus=1`.
- A node may match the feature but still be unavailable due to state, partition policy, or lack of free CPUs/MEM/GPUs.

Related concept: extra constraints
- Slurm also supports `--extra` for matching structured node “extra” data when `SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints` is enabled.
- That is more flexible than plain features because it can match key/value-style metadata.

Operational consequences:
- Over-constraining jobs can make them pend unnecessarily.
- Under-constraining jobs can place them on less preferred hardware.
- Features are especially useful when multiple node types share a partition.

Example:
- Partition has mixed nodes: some with `a100`, some with `v100`.
- `sbatch --partition=gpu --constraint=a100 --gpus=2 job.sh`
- Slurm will try to place the job only on nodes in `gpu` that have the `a100` feature and can satisfy 2 GPUs.

In short: node features control eligibility for placement. Slurm first filters nodes by partition/state/policy and your constraints, then places the job among the remaining candidates.

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Node features are labels attached to nodes that Slurm can use for placement filtering.

How they affect placement:
- If a job requests features, Slurm only considers nodes whose feature set satisfies that request.
- This is typically done with `--constraint` in `sbatch`, `srun`, or `salloc`.
- A stricter feature request narrows the eligible node pool, which can increase queue time.
- If no nodes match the requested features, the job stays pending.

Common uses of features:
- CPU type or microarchitecture
- GPU model
- Interconnect type
- Special hardware like large-memory nodes
- Local SSD / NVMe
- Any site-defined capability label

Typical behavior:
- No feature request: job can run on any otherwise eligible node in the partition/account/QOS limits.
- With feature request: placement is restricted to matching nodes only.
- Multiple requested features usually mean Slurm looks for nodes satisfying all requested constraints unless an OR expression is used.

Conceptually:
- AND-style request: “must have feature A and feature B”
- OR-style request: “feature A or feature B is acceptable”

Why this matters operationally:
- Features are a placement filter, not extra resources by themselves.
- Asking for a feature does not create capacity; it only limits where the job may land.
- Overly specific constraints are a common reason for long pending times.

Related but distinct:
- Node features: usually static labels on nodes, used with `--constraint`
- Extra constraints: a separate mechanism using node “Extra” data and `--extra`, if enabled by the site
- Generic resources like GPUs: usually requested with GRES options, not only features

Practical effect on scheduling:
- Slurm first applies normal eligibility rules such as partition, account, limits, and requested resources.
- Then feature constraints reduce the candidate nodes further.
- Placement happens only within that remaining matching set.

Example ideas:
- Request a large-memory feature to force placement on high-memory nodes
- Request a specific GPU-generation feature to avoid older GPU nodes
- Use OR constraints when multiple hardware classes are acceptable to improve start chances

If you want, I can also explain the exact `--constraint` expression syntax Slurm supports.

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
In Slurm, node features are labels attached to nodes that jobs can use as placement constraints.

What features are
- Features are arbitrary strings such as `gpu`, `avx512`, `ib`, `zen4`, `scratch`, or site-specific labels.
- Admins define them on nodes in `slurm.conf`, and some sites also manage changeable/rebootable features through NodeFeatures plugins.
- A node can have multiple features.

How they affect placement
- A job can request features with constraints, typically via `--constraint=...`.
- Slurm then filters eligible nodes to only those whose features satisfy that constraint.
- Features affect node selection before CPU/memory/task allocation details are applied.

Basic behavior
- If you request one feature, only nodes with that feature are eligible.
- If you request multiple features, Slurm evaluates the expression and narrows placement accordingly.
- Fewer eligible nodes usually means longer queue time, especially if the requested combination is rare.

Common constraint patterns
- Single feature: node must have that feature.
- AND-style request: node must satisfy all requested features.
- OR-style request: node may satisfy any of the listed features.
- Counts / more advanced expressions may be supported depending on syntax and site configuration.

Practical impact on scheduling
- Good use of features:
  - targets hardware you actually need
  - avoids unsuitable nodes
  - can improve reproducibility
- Over-constraining:
  - reduces eligible nodes
  - can make jobs stay pending longer
  - may block jobs even when the partition has idle nodes that do not match the feature request

Important distinction
- Features are not the same as partitions.
- Partitions are scheduler groupings of nodes and policy.
- Features are labels used to further filter nodes within the allowed partition(s).

Changeable vs always-active features
- Slurm docs note that some features can be managed by NodeFeatures plugins and may be available but not currently active.
- In those environments, requesting such features can trigger node state changes such as reboot-based activation, depending on site setup.
- Features not managed that way are simply treated as always active labels.

Related concept: extra constraints
- Slurm also supports “extra constraints,” which are separate from normal node features.
- Those use additional node metadata and can further filter placement if enabled by the site.

Typical examples
- `--constraint=gpu` → place only on nodes labeled `gpu`
- `--constraint=avx512` → place only on nodes with AVX-512-capable labeling
- `--constraint=ib` → prefer/require nodes with InfiniBand if that feature is defined

Bottom line
- Node features are scheduler-visible labels on nodes.
- Jobs use them to restrict where they can run.
- They directly affect placement by shrinking or shaping the eligible node set, which can improve fit but also increase pending time if the constraint is too narrow.

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
In Slurm, node features are labels attached to nodes that jobs can request to control placement.

How they affect placement:
- If a job requests a feature, Slurm only considers nodes that match that feature expression.
- This narrows the eligible node set before normal scheduling decisions like partition, CPUs, memory, GPUs, QOS, and priority.

Common uses of features:
- Hardware type: `intel`, `amd`, `zen4`
- Accelerator type: `a100`, `h100`
- Interconnect or storage: `infiniband`, `nvme`
- Software/image state: `cuda12`, `centos9`
- Special capabilities: `largemem`

Typical request syntax:
- `--constraint=<feature>`
- Example: `--constraint=a100`
- Multiple features can be combined in a feature expression, so placement is limited to nodes satisfying that expression.

Practical effect on scheduling:
- More specific feature constraints reduce the number of eligible nodes.
- That can increase pending time if few nodes match.
- If no nodes match, the job will stay pending with a reason related to constraints or unavailable resources.

Important distinction:
- Features are placement filters, not resources by themselves.
- Requesting `--constraint=a100` says “place me on nodes labeled a100.”
- It does not automatically request a GPU count; that still needs resource options such as GPU requests when appropriate.

Related behavior:
- Features can be static labels or site-managed/changeable features.
- On some systems, certain features may be tied to rebootable configurations, but that depends on site configuration.

In short: node features are scheduler-visible tags, and they affect placement by restricting which nodes are eligible to run the job.

results.prompt: Explain --licenses requests and license pools in Slurm
results.agent_response:
In Slurm, `--licenses` lets a job reserve consumable software license counts the same way it reserves CPUs or GPUs.

- Submit syntax:
  - `sbatch --licenses=ansys:2 job.sh`
  - `srun --licenses=matlab:1 ...`
  - Short form: `-L ansys:2`

What it means:
- The job requests 2 units of the `ansys` license pool.
- Slurm will only start the job when those licenses are available.
- While the job runs, those licenses are counted as in use by Slurm.

License pools:
- A license pool is a named consumable resource with a total count, such as:
  - `ansys:100`
  - `fluent:30`
- Slurm tracks:
  - total
  - used
  - free
- Admins can define them as:
  - local licenses in `slurm.conf`
  - remote/accounting-managed licenses via `sacctmgr`

Typical behavior:
- If enough licenses are free, the job can start.
- If not, the job stays pending until the requested count becomes available.
- The request is cluster-wide unless the site has more specific policy/configuration around how licenses are shared.

Examples:
- `--licenses=matlab:1` → need 1 MATLAB license
- `--licenses=abaqus:4` → need 4 ABAQUS licenses
- Multiple licenses can be requested together, depending on site support/config:
  - `--licenses=ansys:2,matlab:1`

Important distinction:
- `--licenses` is for named software-license resources.
- It is not the same as CPUs, memory, or GPUs.
- It also differs from generic consumable resources unless your site maps licenses into TRES/accounting.

Related admin concepts:
- Local licenses are defined in `slurm.conf` with `Licenses=...`
- Sites can expose them with `scontrol show lic`
- Licenses may also be tracked as TRES if configured, which affects accounting/reporting and sometimes alternative request syntax.

Practical mental model:
- A license pool is a semaphore with a fixed count.
- Jobs decrement the pool when they start and release it when they finish.

If you want, I can also explain:
- how pending reasons look when licenses block a job,
- the difference between local vs remote licenses,
- or how `--licenses` interacts with TRES accounting.
